title: Week 4 · Parts of speech and named entities

lines: Week four moves from one label per text to one label per word.
Part-of-speech tagging gives every word its grammatical role in this sentence.
Book that flight: book is a verb. Hand me that book: book is a noun. The tag depends on context.
Back can even be five things: an adjective, a noun, a verb, a particle or an adverb.
Open classes gain new words every day: nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs. Selfie, to google.
Closed classes almost never change: determiners, pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions, auxiliaries.
Universal Dependencies has seventeen tags in total.
Only a small share of word types is ambiguous, but those are the common words.
Take book book book cat dog. One of three types is ambiguous, but three of five tokens are.
The simplest tagger gives each word its most frequent tag from training. It ignores context, so book a flight comes out wrong.
Better taggers combine three clues: the word itself, its neighbours, and its shape, like a suffix or a capital letter. A clue is not a rule: friendly ends in l y and is an adjective.
Named entity recognition finds names of things: people, organizations, locations, geo-political entities.
It is harder than part-of-speech tagging for two reasons.
First, segmentation: United Airlines Holding is one entity of three words.
Second, type ambiguity: Washington can be a person, a team, a place or a state, and only the context decides.
To label entities word by word, we use B I O. B begins an entity, I is inside it, O is outside.
Jane, B person. Villanueva, I person. Of, O. United, B organization.
With n entity types, B I O needs two n plus one tags. Three types give seven.
I O uses n plus one tags, but cannot separate two people standing next to each other. B I O E S adds end and single, for four n plus one.
